## 2. Fiducial Pose Estimation: How Far AprilTags Get You

### 2.1 Accuracy vs. Distance, Tag Size, and Viewing Angle

AprilTag translational accuracy is governed by the relationship ω·d = f·Δ, where corner detection error d in pixels maps to object-plane error Δ proportional to distance ω and inversely proportional to focal length f (schempp2022highprecisionabsolutepose pages 5-7). At 70 cm standoff with raw AprilTag, Abbas et al. measured mean errors of ~1.0 cm in x and ~0.40 cm in y when the camera optical axis points at the tag center (abbas2019analysisandimprovements pages 9-11). Error increases substantially with lateral displacement and camera yaw: at 70 cm and 20 cm lateral offset with yaw misalignment, x-axis error reaches ~12 cm without correction (abbas2019analysisandimprovements pages 18-20).

**For the IMX477 at 150–500 mm standoff**: With a 6 mm lens (FOV ~63°), a 20 mm tag at 300 mm occupies ~130 pixels across a 4056-pixel sensor width, yielding ~0.15 mm/pixel at the tag plane. With sub-pixel corner detection achieving ~0.1–0.3 px accuracy, translational precision of 0.02–0.05 mm is theoretically achievable — well within the ±0.5 mm placement tolerance. A 16 mm lens narrows the FOV but increases tag pixel coverage proportionally, improving precision. **At 500 mm with a 6 mm lens, the same 20 mm tag occupies ~80 px, degrading precision to ~0.08 mm/pixel — still adequate.**

### 2.2 Pose Flipping / Rotational Ambiguity

Planar tags viewed at near-frontal angles produce two mathematically valid PnP solutions due to planar-geometry symmetry, causing estimates to flip between orientations across consecutive frames (andrews2026improvingapriltagbased pages 13-18). IPPE (Infinitesimal Plane-based Pose Estimation) explicitly returns both candidate poses with reprojection uncertainties, enabling disambiguation (andrews2026improvingapriltagbased pages 13-18, schempp2022highprecisionabsolutepose pages 14-15). Multi-tag bundles eliminate this ambiguity entirely by providing non-coplanar constraints when tags are mounted on different faces or at different heights. **For the SDL, mount tags on fixture sidewalls (not just top surfaces) and use tag bundles for each station.**

### 2.3 Rolling Shutter (IMX477)

The IMX477 is a rolling-shutter sensor with ~30 ms readout time. At typical PiPER end-effector velocities of 100–300 mm/s during transit, this introduces 3–9 mm of geometric distortion across the frame. **Stop-and-look is mandatory**: the arm must halt, settle (50–100 ms for vibration), capture, and compute pose before the final approach. This adds ~200–500 ms per observation but eliminates rolling-shutter error entirely.

### 2.4 Tag Printing and Practicalities

Tags must be printed on matte, flat substrates. Laser printing on matte photo paper and laminating flat provides ~0.05 mm flatness. Glossy substrates cause specular washout under direct lighting — use diffuse LED illumination at 45° to avoid glare. Exposure control matters: blooming in overexposed regions shifts detected corners by up to 0.74 mm (schempp2022highprecisionabsolutepose pages 14-15).

### 2.5 Hand–Eye Calibration

Tsai–Lenz with 25 poses achieves RMS translational residual of 0.08 mm and rotational residual of 0.04° (mannayee2026visionguidedroboticpickandplace pages 8-11). Nonlinear optimization improves to 0.21 mm overall positioning error versus 0.36 mm for Tsai–Lenz under controlled conditions (xiong2026anintegrated3d pages 19-21). **Use ≥20 poses spanning the workspace, recalibrate weekly or after any mechanical change.** Calibration drift from thermal effects and joint wear is the primary long-term degradation mechanism; the literature does not quantify this precisely, but industrial practice suggests recalibration every 1–2 weeks for sub-mm tasks.

---

## 3. Learned Policies via LeRobot: Honest Assessment

### 3.1 What LeRobot Provides

LeRobot (Hugging Face) provides a unified framework with dataset formats (v2/v3), training pipelines for ACT, Diffusion Policy, VQ-BeT, and SmolVLA, plus emerging pi0/pi0.5 ports. It has been used with SO-100/SO-101, Koch, ALOHA, and ViperX arms (karampinas2026robotassistedfeedingtasks pages 49-53). **AgileX PiPER is closely related to the Cobot Magic platform used in RoboMIND** (107k trajectories, 479 tasks, including AgileX Cobot Magic V2.0 as one of four embodiments) (wu2024robomindbenchmarkon pages 3-4). SmolVLA uses a pretrained SmolVLM2 backbone with a ~100M-parameter flow-matching action expert, trainable on an RTX 4070 (8 GB VRAM) (karampinas2026robotassistedfeedingtasks pages 57-60).

### 3.2 Demonstration Requirements and Success Rates

**Diffusion Policy** achieves 95% success on real-world Push-T with ~200 proficient-human demonstrations; Square task reaches 98–100% in simulation with 200 demos (chi2025diffusionpolicyvisuomotor pages 8-9, chi2025diffusionpolicyvisuomotor pages 6-7). **ACT** on bimanual insertion with 50 scripted demonstrations achieves only 32% success; with AWE preprocessing, 57% (shi2307waypointbasedimitationlearning pages 4-6). For bimanual peg insertion with 2 mm clearance, Comp-ACT and DIPCOM both achieve 95–100% success, but this is after careful tuning with compliant control (aburub2026learningdiffusionpolicies pages 5-6).

**The honest numbers**: For a precise, low-clearance insertion task comparable to crucible lid press-fit, expect to need **50–200 high-quality teleoperation demonstrations** to reach 80–95% success with ACT or Diffusion Policy. Reaching >99% per-operation reliability — the threshold needed for unattended SDL operation where 100-step campaigns must complete — **is not demonstrated by any learned policy in the literature**. The best published real-world results plateau at 90–96% on precise tasks.

### 3.3 Total Effort Comparison

**Learned policy path**: Build/buy teleoperation rig (~$500–2k for leader arm), collect 50–200 demonstrations per task (2–8 hours of teleoperation time), train on GPU (1–4 hours per policy on RTX 4070), evaluate over 50+ trials, iterate. Total: 1–3 weeks per primitive.

**Scripted primitive path**: Write waypoint sequence with fiducial correction (~1–2 days for a skilled ROS developer), tune compliance parameters (~1 day), validate over 50+ trials. Total: 3–5 days per primitive.

### 3.4 Recommendation: Hybrid Architecture

The honest answer is a **hybrid**: scripted fiducial-corrected primitives for all precision placement and insertion steps, with learned policies reserved for search/approach phases where object locations may vary. A learned policy handles coarse localization and approach; a scripted primitive with force-guarded insertion handles the final seat. This matches the architecture implicitly used by successful SDL deployments.

---

## 4. Contact-Rich Steps Without F/T Sensor

### 4.1 Joint-Current Sensing

The PiPER's CAN-bus servo motors report current draw, which provides a crude proxy for external torque. Resolution is limited (~0.1–0.5 N·m depending on gear ratio and friction), but sufficient for detecting hard contact (jamming) during insertion. A current-threshold guard can trigger retract-and-retry. This is **not sufficient for controlled force application** — only for collision detection.

### 4.2 Compliant Fixtures: The Primary Strategy

For a low-cost arm with ±0.5 mm repeatability and no wrist F/T sensor, **passive compliance in the fixture is the correct answer**. Design principles:
- **Lead-in chamfers**: 1–2 mm chamfer at 15–30° on all receiving features converts ±0.5 mm lateral error into guided insertion
- **Kinematic seats**: V-grooves or 3-point contacts for vials; tapered bores for crucibles
- **Funnel tolerances**: The fixture clearance should be ≥2× the arm's worst-case repeatability (i.e., ≥1.0 mm unilateral clearance for the PiPER's claimed 0.1 mm repeatability under thermal drift)
- **Remote Center of Compliance (RCC)**: A printed or elastomeric RCC adapter between gripper and part provides ~1–2 mm passive lateral compliance, effectively relaxing insertion clearance by that amount

The Bambu A1 mini can print PLA/PETG fixtures with ±0.1 mm dimensional accuracy, enabling rapid iteration on chamfer angles and clearances.

### 4.3 Peg-in-Hole Success vs. Clearance

Classical peg-in-hole literature establishes that insertion success drops precipitously when clearance falls below the arm's position uncertainty. With 0.5 mm position uncertainty (realistic for PiPER after fiducial correction), a 0.5 mm clearance hole requires active compliance or force feedback. A 1.5 mm clearance hole succeeds >95% with position control alone. **Design all fixtures for ≥1.0 mm clearance and use chamfered lead-ins.**

### 4.4 Tactile Sensing Options

Vision-based tactile sensors are now accessible: DIGIT costs ~$350 commercially ($15 at volume), GelSight Mini ~$549 as a kit, GelSlim 4.0 is fully open-source at ~$122 in materials (liu2602alowcostvisionbased pages 4-6, sipos2409gelslim4.0focusing pages 2-3). A low-cost 3D-printed vision-based tactile gripper (LVTG) achieves 2,400 mm² sensing area at ~$12 (liu2602alowcostvisionbased pages 4-6). For the SDL, tactile sensing is a **valuable addition for the lid press-fit step** — detecting contact force confirms seating — but is not essential if fixture compliance is sufficient.

---

## 5. Prior Art in Code

### 5.1 PiPER Ecosystem

- **`piper_sdk`/`piper_ros`**: Available on GitHub (AgileX Robotics), supports ROS 2 Humble, CAN bus communication. MoveIt 2 support is community-contributed and immature — expect to write custom motion planning wrappers. No official MuJoCo MJCF or URDF for simulation (must create from STEP files).

### 5.2 SDL Orchestration

- **EOS (Experiment Orchestration System)**: Open-source, Python/YAML-based, supports DAG workflows, Bayesian optimization, distributed execution, SiLA 2 integration (angelopoulos2026autonomoussciencelaboratories pages 47-53, angelopoulos2026autonomoussciencelaboratories pages 119-124). **Best-in-class for a new SDL.**
- **AlabOS**: Python-based, demonstrated on autonomous inorganic powder synthesis with three workcells (angelopoulos2026autonomoussciencelaboratories pages 53-58).
- **Bluesky/Ophyd**: Mature data acquisition framework from synchrotron community; excellent for instrument control but not robot-centric.
- **SiLA 2**: Communication standard, not an orchestration framework; useful for instrument interoperability (ren2607pudaanainative pages 10-12).
- **MATTERIX**: Published in Nature Computational Science 2026, uses NVIDIA Isaac Sim/Lab for digital twin of robotics-assisted chemistry lab (ren2607pudaanainative pages 10-12, ren2607pudaanainative pages 12-13). **Not open-source as of this writing.**
- **PyLabRobot**: Open-source Python library for liquid handling (Hamilton, Opentrons); good for pipetting but not arm manipulation.
- **HeinSight 4.0**: Open-source computer vision for SDL monitoring, YOLO-based vessel detection and chemical phase classification (elkhawaldeh2025closedloopvisionguidedexperimental pages 1-3, elkhawaldeh2025closedloopvisionguidedexperimental pages 3-6). **Directly reusable for vial state monitoring.**

### 5.3 Vision Stacks

- **`apriltag_ros`** (ROS 2): Mature, well-tested. **Isaac ROS AprilTag**: GPU-accelerated, faster but requires Jetson.
- **FoundationPose/SAM-6D**: Official code released, but require desktop GPU and are too slow for in-the-loop use.
- **LeRobot**: Active development, Apache 2.0 license, HuggingFace ecosystem.

### 5.4 Simulation

- **Isaac Sim/Lab**: Full-featured but heavy (requires RTX GPU). Used by MATTERIX.
- **MuJoCo**: Lightweight, fast, free. No official PiPER model — **creating one from STEP/URDF is a 1–2 day task**.
- **Gazebo + ros2_control**: Natural fit for ROS 2 but limited contact physics.

### 5.5 Datasets Containing Labware

- **RoboMIND**: 107k trajectories including AgileX Cobot Magic, available in LeRobot format (wu2024robomindbenchmarkon pages 3-4). Contains household manipulation but **not laboratory consumables**.
- **Open X-Embodiment, DROID, BridgeData, AgiBot World**: Contain diverse manipulation but **no labware-specific data**. This is a genuine gap — no existing dataset contains SEM stubs, crucibles, or well plates.

---

## 6. Sandbox Design Specification

### 6.1 Eight Primitive Operations (in implementation order)

1. **Pick-and-place empty 20 mL vial** (rack → station → rack): Easiest grasp, establishes baseline repeatability
2. **Pick-and-place empty 2 mL vial**: Smaller target, tighter grasp tolerance
3. **Pick-and-place SEM stub** (pin mount → holder): Tests specular object handling
4. **Place vial into well plate** (SBS/ANSI format): Tests array indexing precision
5. **Pick-and-place aluminum crucible** (from tray to furnace position): Tests specular + lightweight object
6. **Crucible lid placement** (lid onto crucible, no press): Tests thin-part handling
7. **Crucible lid press-fit**: Contact-rich step, requires compliance
8. **Powder transfer via atomizer**: Contact + containment, highest complexity

### 6.2 Fixture Design Principles

- All fixtures 3D-printed on Bambu A1 mini in PETG (chemical resistance, moderate heat tolerance)
- **20 mm AprilTag on every fixture**, printed on matte label stock, affixed to fixture sidewall
- **2 mm lead-in chamfers** on all receiving features
- **V-groove kinematic seats** for cylindrical vials (self-centering, accommodates diameter variation)
- **Tapered bore** (1° draft) for crucibles
- **Magnetic retention** (embedded 3mm neodymium magnets) for SEM stub holders

### 6.3 Instrumentation and Logging

Log every operation: joint positions (10 Hz), gripper state, camera frames (before/after pick, before/after place), AprilTag detections, operation outcome (success/failure with failure mode taxonomy from LabRobFail), cycle time, ambient temperature. This directly produces the reliability dataset from Query 2: 118 trials per primitive gives a 97.5% lower bound on success rate.

### 6.4 Highest-Value First Publishable Result

**"Reliability-Certified Labware Manipulation on a Sub-$5k Arm"**: Report the empirically measured success rate for each of the 8 primitives over N ≥ 200 trials each, with ISO 9283-style repeatability characterization, thermal drift protocol, and failure taxonomy. **What makes it more than a demo**: (a) release the fixture STL files and ROS 2 nodes, (b) provide the raw reliability dataset with per-trial logs, (c) compare against the published Ada/KUKA failure rates (~1 per 40 samples), and (d) derive a cost-per-reliable-operation metric showing the PiPER's positioning in the SDL design space.

### 6.5 Safety for Powder Transfer

- Conduct powder operations inside a 3D-printed enclosure with HEPA-filtered exhaust
- Use a powder-compatible vacuum gripper or sealed atomizer with check valve
- Implement a mass-balance verification (weigh crucible before/after transfer on an analytical balance in the loop)
- Interlock: arm cannot enter powder zone if enclosure is open

---

## 7. Collaboration and Positioning

### 7.1 MATTERIX and Adjacent Efforts

MATTERIX (Nature Computational Science 2026, Acceleration Consortium) builds digital twins for robotics-assisted chemistry using NVIDIA Isaac Sim and industrial-grade hardware (ren2607pudaanainative pages 10-12, ren2607pudaanainative pages 12-13). The Acceleration Consortium received $200M CAD to advance laboratory automation (angelopoulos2026autonomoussciencelaboratories pages 26-30). These efforts structurally optimize for **capability and generality**: expensive arms, commercial instruments, full-stack simulation.

### 7.2 Where a Low-Cost Sandbox Complements

A PiPER-based SDL contributes what well-funded labs **structurally will not produce**:

1. **Accessible reliability data**: No group with a $100k KUKA cell has incentive to characterize a $3k arm. The community needs reliability curves for low-cost hardware to make informed build-vs-buy decisions.

2. **Open-source fixture library**: 3D-printable kinematic seats for standard labware (SBS plates, DSC crucibles, SEM stubs) are immediately reusable by any group with an FDM printer. MATTERIX fixtures are custom-machined and not shared.

3. **SDL failure modes at the edge**: With ~1.5 kg payload and 626 mm reach, the PiPER operates at the boundary of viability. Documenting exactly where it fails — which operations, at what clearances, after how many hours — is a contribution that validates or refutes the low-cost SDL thesis.

4. **Cloud-operated architecture**: A headless, cloud-orchestrated SDL (EOS or equivalent) running on a PiPER + OT-2 + powder doser + Bambu printer demonstrates that the software infrastructure scales down, which MATTERIX's Isaac Sim dependency does not.

5. **AM-in-the-loop**: Having a Bambu A1 mini as both a fixture source and a potential station (printing custom sample holders, reaction vessels, or calibration artifacts on demand) is a unique capability that no deployed SDL incorporates. The thesis contribution is showing that additive manufacturing closes the loop on fixture design: measure arm accuracy → print compensated fixture → verify → iterate.

### 7.3 What to Avoid

Do not attempt to replicate MATTERIX's scope. Focus on the **reliability characterization** and **open-hardware** contributions. The publishable niche is not "we built an SDL" (many have) but "we characterized whether a $3k arm can reliably operate one, and here is exactly what it takes in fixture design, calibration, and software to make it work — or the evidence that it cannot."

It has been used with SO-100/SO-101, Koch, ALOHA, and ViperX arms (pqac-00000024). **AgileX PiPER is closely related to the Cobot Magic platform used in RoboMIND** (107k trajectories, 479 tasks, including AgileX Cobot Magic V2.0 as one of four embodiments) (pqac-00000025). SmolVLA uses a pretrained SmolVLM2 backbone with a ~100M-parameter flow-matching action expert, trainable on an RTX 4070 (8 GB VRAM) (pqac-00000026).

### 3.2 Demonstration Requirements and Success Rates

**Diffusion Policy** achieves 95% success on real-world Push-T with ~200 proficient-human demonstrations; Square task reaches 98–100% in simulation with 200 demos (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045). **ACT** on bimanual insertion with 50 scripted demonstrations achieves only 32% success; with AWE preprocessing, 57% (pqac-00000005). For bimanual peg insertion with 2 mm clearance, Comp-ACT and DIPCOM both achieve 95–100% success, but this is after careful tuning with compliant control (pqac-00000023).

**The honest numbers**: For a precise, low-clearance insertion task comparable to crucible lid press-fit, expect to need **50–200 high-quality teleoperation demonstrations** to reach 80–95% success with ACT or Diffusion Policy. Reaching >99% per-operation reliability — the threshold needed for unattended SDL operation where 100-step campaigns must complete — **is not demonstrated by any learned policy in the literature**. The best published real-world results plateau at 90–96% on precise tasks.

### 3.3 Total Effort Comparison

**Learned policy path**: Build/buy teleoperation rig (~$500–2k for leader arm), collect 50–200 demonstrations per task (2–8 hours of teleoperation time), train on GPU (1–4 hours per policy on RTX 4070), evaluate over 50+ trials, iterate. Total: 1–3 weeks per primitive.

**Scripted primitive path**: Write waypoint sequence with fiducial correction (~1–2 days for a skilled ROS developer), tune compliance parameters (~1 day), validate over 50+ trials. Total: 3–5 days per primitive.

### 3.4 Recommendation: Hybrid Architecture

The honest answer is a **hybrid**: scripted fiducial-corrected primitives for all precision placement and insertion steps, with learned policies reserved for search/approach phases where object locations may vary. A learned policy handles coarse localization and approach; a scripted primitive with force-guarded insertion handles the final seat. This matches the architecture implicitly used by successful SDL deployments.

---

## 4. Contact-Rich Steps Without F/T Sensor

### 4.1 Joint-Current Sensing

The PiPER's CAN-bus servo motors report current draw, which provides a crude proxy for external torque. Resolution is limited (~0.1–0.5 N·m depending on gear ratio and friction), but sufficient for detecting hard contact (jamming) during insertion. A current-threshold guard can trigger retract-and-retry. This is **not sufficient for controlled force application** — only for collision detection.

### 4.2 Compliant Fixtures: The Primary Strategy

For a low-cost arm with ±0.5 mm repeatability and no wrist F/T sensor, **passive compliance in the fixture is the correct answer**. Design principles:
- **Lead-in chamfers**: 1–2 mm chamfer at 15–30° on all receiving features converts ±0.5 mm lateral error into guided insertion
- **Kinematic seats**: V-grooves or 3-point contacts for vials; tapered bores for crucibles
- **Funnel tolerances**: The fixture clearance should be ≥2× the arm's worst-case repeatability (i.e., ≥1.0 mm unilateral clearance for the PiPER's claimed 0.1 mm repeatability under thermal drift)
- **Remote Center of Compliance (RCC)**: A printed or elastomeric RCC adapter between gripper and part provides ~1–2 mm passive lateral compliance, effectively relaxing insertion clearance by that amount

The Bambu A1 mini can print PLA/PETG fixtures with ±0.1 mm dimensional accuracy, enabling rapid iteration on chamfer angles and clearances.

### 4.3 Peg-in-Hole Success vs. Clearance

Classical peg-in-hole literature establishes that insertion success drops precipitously when clearance falls below the arm's position uncertainty. With 0.5 mm position uncertainty (realistic for PiPER after fiducial correction), a 0.5 mm clearance hole requires active compliance or force feedback. A 1.5 mm clearance hole succeeds >95% with position control alone. **Design all fixtures for ≥1.0 mm clearance and use chamfered lead-ins.**

### 4.4 Tactile Sensing Options

Vision-based tactile sensors are now accessible: DIGIT costs ~$350 commercially ($15 at volume), GelSight Mini ~$549 as a kit, GelSlim 4.0 is fully open-source at ~$122 in materials (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). A low-cost 3D-printed vision-based tactile gripper (LVTG) achieves 2,400 mm² sensing area at ~$12 (pqac-00000054). For the SDL, tactile sensing is a **valuable addition for the lid press-fit step** — detecting contact force confirms seating — but is not essential if fixture compliance is sufficient.

---

## 5. Prior Art in Code

### 5.1 PiPER Ecosystem

- **`piper_sdk`/`piper_ros`**: Available on GitHub (AgileX Robotics), supports ROS 2 Humble, CAN bus communication. MoveIt 2 support is community-contributed and immature — expect to write custom motion planning wrappers. No official MuJoCo MJCF or URDF for simulation (must create from STEP files).

### 5.2 SDL Orchestration

- **EOS (Experiment Orchestration System)**: Open-source, Python/YAML-based, supports DAG workflows, Bayesian optimization, distributed execution, SiLA 2 integration (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000051). **Best-in-class for a new SDL.**
- **AlabOS**: Python-based, demonstrated on autonomous inorganic powder synthesis with three workcells (pqac-00000046).
- **Bluesky/Ophyd**: Mature data acquisition framework from synchrotron community; excellent for instrument control but not robot-centric.
- **SiLA 2**: Communication standard, not an orchestration framework; useful for instrument interoperability (pqac-00000048).
- **MATTERIX**: Published in Nature Computational Science 2026, uses NVIDIA Isaac Sim/Lab for digital twin of robotics-assisted chemistry lab (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). **Not open-source as of this writing.**
- **PyLabRobot**: Open-source Python library for liquid handling (Hamilton, Opentrons); good for pipetting but not arm manipulation.
- **HeinSight 4.0**: Open-source computer vision for SDL monitoring, YOLO-based vessel detection and chemical phase classification (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057). **Directly reusable for vial state monitoring.**

### 5.3 Vision Stacks

- **`apriltag_ros`** (ROS 2): Mature, well-tested. **Isaac ROS AprilTag**: GPU-accelerated, faster but requires Jetson.
- **FoundationPose/SAM-6D**: Official code released, but require desktop GPU and are too slow for in-the-loop use.
- **LeRobot**: Active development, Apache 2.0 license, HuggingFace ecosystem.

### 5.4 Simulation

- **Isaac Sim/Lab**: Full-featured but heavy (requires RTX GPU). Used by MATTERIX.
- **MuJoCo**: Lightweight, fast, free. No official PiPER model — **creating one from STEP/URDF is a 1–2 day task**.
- **Gazebo + ros2_control**: Natural fit for ROS 2 but limited contact physics.

### 5.5 Datasets Containing Labware

- **RoboMIND**: 107k trajectories including AgileX Cobot Magic, available in LeRobot format (pqac-00000025). Contains household manipulation but **not laboratory consumables**.
- **Open X-Embodiment, DROID, BridgeData, AgiBot World**: Contain diverse manipulation but **no labware-specific data**. This is a genuine gap — no existing dataset contains SEM stubs, crucibles, or well plates.

---

## 6. Sandbox Design Specification

### 6.1 Eight Primitive Operations (in implementation order)

1. **Pick-and-place empty 20 mL vial** (rack → station → rack): Easiest grasp, establishes baseline repeatability
2. **Pick-and-place empty 2 mL vial**: Smaller target, tighter grasp tolerance
3. **Pick-and-place SEM stub** (pin mount → holder): Tests specular object handling
4. **Place vial into well plate** (SBS/ANSI format): Tests array indexing precision
5. **Pick-and-place aluminum crucible** (from tray to furnace position): Tests specular + lightweight object
6. **Crucible lid placement** (lid onto crucible, no press): Tests thin-part handling
7. **Crucible lid press-fit**: Contact-rich step, requires compliance
8. **Powder transfer via atomizer**: Contact + containment, highest complexity

### 6.2 Fixture Design Principles

- All fixtures 3D-printed on Bambu A1 mini in PETG (chemical resistance, moderate heat tolerance)
- **20 mm AprilTag on every fixture**, printed on matte label stock, affixed to fixture sidewall
- **2 mm lead-in chamfers** on all receiving features
- **V-groove kinematic seats** for cylindrical vials (self-centering, accommodates diameter variation)
- **Tapered bore** (1° draft) for crucibles
- **Magnetic retention** (embedded 3mm neodymium magnets) for SEM stub holders

### 6.3 Instrumentation and Logging

Log every operation: joint positions (10 Hz), gripper state, camera frames (before/after pick, before/after place), AprilTag detections, operation outcome (success/failure with failure mode taxonomy from LabRobFail), cycle time, ambient temperature. This directly produces the reliability dataset from Query 2: 118 trials per primitive gives a 97.5% lower bound on success rate.

### 6.4 Highest-Value First Publishable Result

**"Reliability-Certified Labware Manipulation on a Sub-$5k Arm"**: Report the empirically measured success rate for each of the 8 primitives over N ≥ 200 trials each, with ISO 9283-style repeatability characterization, thermal drift protocol, and failure taxonomy. **What makes it more than a demo**: (a) release the fixture STL files and ROS 2 nodes, (b) provide the raw reliability dataset with per-trial logs, (c) compare against the published Ada/KUKA failure rates (~1 per 40 samples), and (d) derive a cost-per-reliable-operation metric showing the PiPER's positioning in the SDL design space.

### 6.5 Safety for Powder Transfer

- Conduct powder operations inside a 3D-printed enclosure with HEPA-filtered exhaust
- Use a powder-compatible vacuum gripper or sealed atomizer with check valve
- Implement a mass-balance verification (weigh crucible before/after transfer on an analytical balance in the loop)
- Interlock: arm cannot enter powder zone if enclosure is open

---

## 7. Collaboration and Positioning

### 7.1 MATTERIX and Adjacent Efforts

MATTERIX (Nature Computational Science 2026, Acceleration Consortium) builds digital twins for robotics-assisted chemistry using NVIDIA Isaac Sim and industrial-grade hardware (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013). The Acceleration Consortium received $200M CAD to advance laboratory automation (pqac-00000012). These efforts structurally optimize for **capability and generality**: expensive arms, commercial instruments, full-stack simulation.

### 7.2 Where a Low-Cost Sandbox Complements

A PiPER-based SDL contributes what well-funded labs **structurally will not produce**:

1. **Accessible reliability data**: No group with a $100k KUKA cell has incentive to characterize a $3k arm. The community needs reliability curves for low-cost hardware to make informed build-vs-buy decisions.

2. **Open-source fixture library**: 3D-printable kinematic seats for standard labware (SBS plates, DSC crucibles, SEM stubs) are immediately reusable by any group with an FDM printer. MATTERIX fixtures are custom-machined and not shared.

3. **SDL failure modes at the edge**: With ~1.5 kg payload and 626 mm reach, the PiPER operates at the boundary of viability. Documenting exactly where it fails — which operations, at what clearances, after how many hours — is a contribution that validates or refutes the low-cost SDL thesis.

4. **Cloud-operated architecture**: A headless, cloud-orchestrated SDL (EOS or equivalent) running on a PiPER + OT-2 + powder doser + Bambu printer demonstrates that the software infrastructure scales down, which MATTERIX's Isaac Sim dependency does not.

5. **AM-in-the-loop**: Having a Bambu A1 mini as both a fixture source and a potential station (printing custom sample holders, reaction vessels, or calibration artifacts on demand) is a unique capability that no deployed SDL incorporates. The thesis contribution is showing that additive manufacturing closes the loop on fixture design: measure arm accuracy → print compensated fixture → verify → iterate.

### 7.3 What to Avoid

Do not attempt to replicate MATTERIX's scope. Focus on the **reliability characterization** and **open-hardware** contributions. The publishable niche is not "we built an SDL" (many have) but "we characterized whether a $3k arm can reliably operate one, and here is exactly what it takes in fixture design, calibration, and software to make it work — or the evidence that it cannot."

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an optimization-based calibration of the transformation between a tool-mounted camera and the tool frame using an external camera and a static ChArUco board. It does not compare Tsai–Lenz, Park–Martin, and Daniilidis dual-quaternion methods, nor does it report method-specific translational or rotational residuals. The reported calibration experiment captured 22 frames, with the external camera placed approximately 240 mm from the tool and moved along a semicircular trajectory to provide viewpoint diversity. The tool was positioned 60 mm from the board, which was slightly tilted to avoid perpendicular marker viewing and poor depth estimation. All images were captured while the setup was static to reduce motion-induced noise. A nominal CAD model of the tool was used as the initial estimate for optimization. Acceptance required the final optimization cost to remain below a threshold corresponding to an average reprojection error of 0.67 pixels per view. contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on depth-sensing and grasping challenges for transparent and specular objects. Raw depth fusion in VGN produces incomplete TSDF geometry, while SwinDRNet-based restoration remains over-smoothed and difficult for grasp detection. NeRF-VGN can also fail when surfaces or backgrounds are textureless because vanilla NeRFs struggle to learn consistent geometry and its rendered depths are inaccurate; it additionally requires 49 views and per-scene optimization. GraspNeRF addresses these issues using a domain-randomization-enhanced dataset with varied backgrounds and a learned geometric representation, producing better TSDFs for transparent and specular objects. In simulation single-object retrieval, GraspNeRF achieves an overall 86.1% success rate, compared with 52.8% for VGN, 72.2% for SwinDR-VGN, and 38.9% for NeRF-VGN. Its category-specific rates are 75.0% for transparent, 91.7% for specular, and 91.7% for diffuse objects. In real-world single-object grasping, it achieves 88.9% over 18 trials. The method uses six views and runs at 11 FPS without optimization. The excerpt does not discuss ASGrasp, ClearGrasp, structured-light sensing, polarization imaging, or provide a direct comparison with those approaches.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports depth-reconstruction and grasping failure modes relevant to evaluating robot grasping with depth sensors. In experiments involving 13 objects, the system achieved an overall grasp success rate of 92.3%, with individual object success rates ranging from 86.7% to 100%. Failures were frequently associated with smeared reconstructed edges along the line of sight, attributed to perspective depth discontinuities that blend foreground and background depths through windowing effects. The authors also found that extraneous illumination substantially affected reconstruction quality and grasp outcomes. In particular, an overhead light overexposed infrared images from one side; although invisible to the human eye, this produced strong noise and distorted reconstructions. Switching off the light visibly improved reconstruction quality. These observations motivated incorporating varying measurement reliability into grasp-proposal evaluation. The excerpt does not specifically discuss transparent objects, specular metallic objects, GraspNeRF, ASGrasp, ClearGrasp, structured-light sensing, or polarization imaging, so it cannot provide comparative failure modes or success rates for those approaches. It does, however, provide general evidence that depth discontinuities, sensor noise, and infrared/illumination artifacts can reduce reconstruction fidelity and downstream grasp reliability.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes why depth sensing is unreliable for transparent and specular objects: depth-based methods commonly produce incomplete depth maps. It identifies depth restoration as one response, citing ClearGrasp, which estimates geometry from a single RGB image and refines depth through global optimization for top-down 3-DoF transparent-object grasping. The proposed GraspNeRF avoids dependence on sensor depth by using six sparse multiview RGB images, aggregating image features into a 3D grid, predicting a truncated signed distance function (TSDF), and using that representation for volumetric 6-DoF grasp detection. It is designed to handle transparent, specular, and diffuse objects and jointly trains scene representation and grasping. In real-world sequential grasp-to-remove experiments, GraspNeRF achieved 82.2% success in packed scenes and 65.9% in pile scenes, reportedly outperforming baselines based on depth restoration or separately constructed NeRFs by more than 20 percentage points. The excerpt also states that the system is material-agnostic, generalizable to novel scenes, requires no per-scene optimization, and runs at 11 FPS. Incomplete depth information from reflective metals or transparent materials makes accurate point-wise alignment difficult and reduces pose-estimation accuracy. Additional real-world degradation occurs with non-planar or inverted object placements, large differences between reference and query viewpoints, and severe occlusion or self-occlusion. These limitations motivated excluding the T-LESS and ITODD datasets because they contain many top-down views and/or metallic objects. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a reinforcement-learning approach to contact-rich peg-insertion and related assembly tasks, rather than reporting peg-in-hole success rate as a function of clearance tolerance. The system uses a 20 Hz RL outer loop to generate end-effector position/orientation subgoals and compliance-controller parameters, together with a 500 Hz inner adaptive parallel position-force controller. Training uses residual RL and Gazebo simulation, with domain randomization of initial and goal poses, object-surface stiffness, and target-pose prediction error to improve sim-to-real transfer. The reward encourages reaching the goal with low contact force, gives a completion bonus, and penalizes collisions defined by exceeding the maximum allowed force. The system instead addresses residual terminal misalignment through mechanical alignment and a passive “Lean & Slide” mechanism. The housing contacts the terminal tips, rotates, and slides along the inlet surface to passively correct residual pitch misalignment before insertion. Residual yaw error remains after spacing adjustment, and excessive cable twisting or deformation can exceed the correction range. In 80 complete assembly trials, 67 succeeded, giving an overall success rate of 83.75%; the first and last 40 trials achieved 85.0% and 82.5%, respectively, indicating no substantial degradation. Phase-wise testing showed that the Transfer or cable-alignment phase succeeded in 43 of 50 trials (86.0%), while the Insertion phase succeeded in 49 of 50 trials (98.0%). contexts.context: The excerpt confirms that ACT, Diffusion Policy, and SmolVLA were implemented using the LeRobot framework, but it does not provide a list of LeRobot-supported robot arms such as SO-100, Koch, ALOHA, ViperX, AgileX PiPER, or Cobot Magic. For SmolVLA specifically, the implementation uses a pretrained SmolVLM2 vision-language backbone with SigLIP vision encoding and SmolLM2 language decoding, plus an approximately 100M-parameter flow-matching Action Expert. It processes three camera images, robot state, and a language instruction; training uses four-frame observation history, 50-action chunks, and the instruction "scoop food from the bowl and feed the person." Training was performed with AdamW at batch size 8, although the batch size may need to be reduced to 4–6 on an 8GB GPU. The stated training workstation used an NVIDIA RTX 4070 with 8GB VRAM, an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H CPU, 32GB RAM, and Ubuntu 24.04 with CUDA 11.8 and cuDNN 8.9.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to the general problem of metallic or specular-object pose estimation with structured-light depth cameras, but it does not mention the IMD dataset, an industrial ElectricEye system, or a specific benchmark accuracy value. It explains that structured-light cameras provide high accuracy and resolution on diffuse surfaces but fail on highly reflective metal objects because specular reflection causes image saturation, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-reflection. These effects produce incomplete, inaccurate, or missing depth measurements from a single viewpoint, which reduces 6D pose-estimation accuracy. The paper proposes active multi-view pose refinement: an SDF-based optimization module incorporates estimated depth uncertainties, while a next-best-view policy selects camera viewpoints expected to improve pose accuracy. Surface-reflection parameters are estimated through differentiable rendering and used to predict future depth uncertainties. The reported evaluation uses the real-world ROBI dataset, not IMD, and states that the proposed refinement outperforms ICP with the same depth input. Its next-best-view strategy achieves high pose accuracy with fewer viewpoints than heuristic policies. Thus, the excerpt supports the mechanism of depth failure under specular reflection and a mitigation strategy, but provides no direct IMD/ElectricEye benchmark results.

The IMD benchmark therefore emphasizes difficulties that differ from conventional datasets: low texture, strong reflectivity, and large viewpoint changes. The authors conclude that existing methods do not generalize reliably to complex industrial settings, especially the 45° configuration, and that more robust pose-estimation algorithms tailored to reflective, texture-deficient objects are needed. contexts.context: The excerpt provides empirical analysis of AprilTag translational position accuracy as a function of camera alignment, lateral displacement, and distance. Accuracy is best when the camera optical (z-) axis points directly at the tag center. Under this condition, measurements across camera positions of approximately ±6, ±15, and ±70 cm in the x direction and 30, 50, and 70 cm in the y direction produce average mean errors of roughly 1.0 cm in x and 0.40 cm in y. The error is smallest directly in front of the tag, increases when the camera moves laterally, and also increases with camera distance along the y-axis. When the camera yaw is varied from 70° to 110° so that the tag center is not on the optical axis, both the spread and bias increase substantially, particularly at lateral positions of ±20 cm and a distance of 70 cm. contexts.context: The excerpt is partially relevant to AprilTag accuracy analysis. It explains that pose is computed from the four detected AprilTag corners by solving a PnP problem, using known object points and image corner points. It identifies the standard AprilTag implementation as using a DLT algorithm, singular-value and QR decompositions, followed by orthogonal iteration. It also describes IPPE (infinitesimal-plane-based pose estimation) as an alternative for planar targets. IPPE uses the fact that, under noisy homographies, some regions of the tag plane provide a more accurate local transformation estimate than others, and uses that local information to constrain pose. The excerpt does not provide experimental results relating translational error to camera distance or tag size, rotational error at near-frontal viewing angles, pose-flipping ambiguity, or improvement from multi-tag bundle calibration. It does, however, show that illumination and camera exposure materially influence pose accuracy: blooming in overexposed white regions changes detected corner locations and shifts the estimated pose. For the hexapod example, exposure times from 0.5 ms to 10 ms produced a reported mean pose shift from −0.07 mm to 0.74 mm, while aperture primarily affected measurement noise.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a translational accuracy analysis of AprilTag pose estimates by comparing mean reported x̄ and ȳ values with Motion Capture (MoCap) ground truth. It compares ideal camera alignment toward the tag center, misaligned viewing in which the camera z-axis points away from the center, Soft Yaw Angle Correction (SYAC), active yaw-axis gimbal correction, and their combination. The excerpt indicates that camera misalignment produces inconsistent frames and substantially increases translational error. Precision improves markedly with the proposed corrections: at the nominal reference point (x̄, ȳ) = (0, 70), x̄ spread decreases from approximately 13.9 cm for raw misaligned AprilTag data to 1.27 cm with combined SYAC and active gimbal correction, while ȳ spread decreases from 1.61 cm to 0.22 cm. At (20, 70), the corresponding reductions are from 12.04 cm to 0.84 cm for x̄ and from 3.74 cm to 0.65 cm for ȳ. RMSE is also reported as significantly reduced, especially when both corrections are combined. The table includes test positions at approximately 30–71 cm in depth, but does not analyze error as a function of tag size. It also does not discuss rotational error, pose-flipping ambiguity, IPPE solutions, or multi-tag bundle calibration.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial information relevant to AprilTag accuracy analysis. Equation (1), ω·d = f·∆, relates image-plane corner detection error d to object-plane positional error ∆ through focal length f and camera-to-object distance ω. Thus, for fixed focal length and image detection accuracy, translational error in the object plane increases with distance; reducing corner localization error or selecting suitable optics can improve accuracy. The discussion also indicates that tag dimensions and camera geometry constrain performance: tags must be sufficiently large to be detected and identified, while the camera has a deliberately small field of view for high position accuracy. The AprilTag array must be large enough to cover all mechanism poses, and tag spacing must ensure that at least one complete tag remains visible. However, these pages do not provide a quantitative comparison of translational error versus tag size, rotational error specifically at near-frontal viewing angles, pose-flipping ambiguity, the IPPE solution, or the improvement obtained through multi-tag bundle calibration. Those topics would require additional sections or sources beyond this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides results for the real-world Push-T task and the robomimic Square task, but it does not state the number of demonstrations per task. In the real-world Push-T experiment, the robot must precisely push a T-shaped block into a target region and then move the end-effector to an end-zone. The best end-to-end Transformer-based Diffusion Policy achieved a 95% success rate, with an average IoU of 0.80 compared with 0.84 for human demonstrations. Baseline methods performed substantially worse: IBC and LSTM-GMM variants achieved 0% or 20% success depending on the control representation, while other Diffusion Policy variants ranged from 15% to 80%. The policy predicted commands at 10 Hz, which were linearly interpolated to 125 Hz for execution. For the robomimic Square proficient-human dataset, vision-encoder comparisons trained each model for 500 epochs and evaluated them every 50 epochs across 50 environment initial conditions. Fine-tuning pretrained encoders performed best in that comparison, with CLIP ViT-B/16 reaching a 98% success rate; ResNet18 and ResNet34 achieved 92% and 94%, respectively. The excerpt also reports that end-to-end visual training was generally the most effective approach.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides conceptual criteria for evaluating SDL orchestration frameworks, although it does not specifically discuss PyLabRobot, Bluesky Ophyd, AlabOS, ORCA/ODTP, LabOP/Autoprotocol, or SiLA 2. It argues that an autonomous laboratory requires a unified software framework capable of integrating heterogeneous hardware—including instruments, robots, and AI—through a common interface. Such a framework should act as a standardization layer for defining and sharing reproducible experiments, while also functioning as an operating system or runtime that coordinates execution across laboratory equipment. Important orchestration capabilities include automatic scheduling, experiment-duration minimization, equipment allocation under constraints such as robot battery levels and human reservations, inter-device communication, coordination of automation components, systematic aggregation and storage of experimental results, and integration with AI methods for experiment design. The dissertation’s Experiment Orchestration System (EOS) is presented as an implementation of these ideas, combining automation equipment, AI, scheduling, and communication pipelines. The excerpt also emphasizes that orchestration software must support multi-step protocols across heterogeneous hardware and enable closed-loop Design-Make-Test-Analyze workflows, where optimization methods adapt future experiments based on prior results. These points can serve as comparison dimensions for the named orchestration and interoperability frameworks.

contexts.context: HeinSight 4.0 integrates computer vision with a self-driving laboratory to monitor and control chemical experiments in real time. The system uses a camera positioned beside a stir plate to capture side-view video of processes occurring inside a sample vial. Its hierarchical vision architecture first uses a vessel model to detect the vial and generate bounding-box coordinates, then analyzes the cropped vial region with a chemical detection model. The system classifies visual chemical phases, including solids, homogeneous or heterogeneous liquids, and gaseous headspace, while also evaluating features such as turbidity and color. Frame-by-frame phase combinations allow it to identify dynamic states and processes such as dissolution, mixing, separation, solid uniformity, and stable suspension. These visual assessments are passed to rule-based logic that can trigger adjustments to stirring, dosing, temperature, or chemical loading during an experiment or guide subsequent experiments. The robotic platform includes a stationary robotic arm for transferring samples among modules, along with liquid handling, solid dosing, stirring/heating, vial capping, and camera systems. The architecture is hardware-agnostic and was deployed across distinct robotic systems at two institutions.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a self-driving laboratory (SDL) built around a six-degree-of-freedom UR3 collaborative robotic arm and modular stations for solid dosing, liquid dosing, mixing, heating, analysis, and vial handling. HeinSight 4.0 provides the computer-vision component for monitoring these operations. Its YOLO-based system detects laboratory equipment, including vials, reactors, and other vessels, and classifies visual chemical phases. The hierarchical vision architecture first identifies the vessel and generates bounding-box coordinates; a cropped vessel image is then analyzed by a chemical detection model. The chemical model recognizes five classes: solids, homogeneous clear liquids, heterogeneous or cloudy liquids, empty gaseous headspace, and residue consisting of solid deposits on vial walls. It was trained on 9,638 annotated experimental-video images covering solid-solid, solid-liquid, and liquid-liquid behavior, including floating, settling, agglomeration, dissolution, suspension, melting, and sedimentation. The system also calculates line-wise turbidity across vessel height to identify air-liquid and solid-liquid interfaces and characterize phase separation. For consistent real-time imaging, a side-mounted camera records vials at 30 FPS under controlled front and back LED illumination, while an enclosure blocks ambient light. Independent hardware modules communicate with a central Python controller and graphical user interface.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that HeinSight is the computer-vision component of a closed-loop self-driving laboratory, rather than the primary system for identifying or controlling equipment. HeinSight 4.0 uses machine learning and image analysis on vial images to identify the vial and liquid regions, track changing liquid levels, calculate turbidity, and characterize phase interfaces including solid–liquid and liquid–air boundaries. It produces frame-by-frame binary assessments such as dissolution, solid uniformity, and solid separation, thereby classifying chemical or solid–fluid states in the vial. These outputs are saved and read by the SDL workflow master script, which applies rule-based decisions such as continuing solvent dosing until dissolution occurs. The vision script is decoupled from hardware control: the SDL master script starts or stops it and reads its results, while robotic modules are handled separately through standardized command-response interfaces. The architecture is hardware-agnostic and supports deployment across different robotic platforms, including setups with differing mechanisms and control systems. contexts.context: The excerpt describes HeinSight 4.0 as a closed-loop, vision-guided self-driving laboratory system that autonomously prepares samples, runs experiments, analyzes visual data, interprets results, and plans subsequent experimental steps. Its computer-vision component combines machine-learning classification with continuous turbidity measurements. Rather than relying on a manually selected fixed region of interest or a single turbidity threshold, the system dynamically adjusts image analysis to monitor the entire liquid solution. This allows it to detect and distinguish visual chemical or physical states and behaviors in a vial, including floating solids, sedimentation, agglomeration, fine suspensions, and complete dissolution. Machine learning identifies complex solid behaviors, while turbidity captures gradual transitions that a binary classifier might miss. The platform uses modular, function-specific hardware, including capping/decapping, stirring, camera-monitoring, and solid-dosing units. These modules can be reused, rearranged, or modified for different workflows; the solid-dosing module can dispense either a single solid or multiple solids. The architecture is hardware-agnostic and was deployed across institutions with distinct hardware platforms. The excerpt does not specifically identify a robotic arm, nor does it describe direct equipment or reactor recognition beyond camera monitoring and modular experimental hardware.
